articles.title: Listhaug: – Norsk skole er rett og slett en katastrofe
articles.content:
– Vi klarer ikke hjelpe de flinke eller løfte de som er svake. Norsk skole er rett og slett en katastrofe.

Det sier Frp-leder Sylvi Listhaug til NRK torsdag morgen.

Statsminister Jonas Gahr Støre (Ap) mener Frp ikke kan skyve fra seg alt ansvaret, og peker på at partiet hadde finansministeren i flere år.

Listhaug mener at oppsettet i den norske skolen gjør at det er «nærmest umulig» for lærere å strekke til, og mener løsninga er mer nivåinndeling blant elevene.

– Tilpasset opplæring er helt riktig. Hvis elever sliter med lesing, ta dem ut og gi dem ekstra opplæring, sier Støre, men understreker at han ikke mener det er bra å dele inn elevene etter nivå permanent.

Fremskrittspartiet

Fremskrittspartiet er et norsk politisk parti som beskriver seg som liberalistisk. Partiet ble grunnlagt i 1973 som Anders Langes Parti til sterk nedsettelse av skatter, avgifter og offentlige inngrep. Fra 2021 er Sylvi Listhaug partileder.

articles.title: Reuters: Russland øvde på å bruke hemmelig våpen mot undersjøiske kabler – hindret av Norge og Nato
articles.content:
Russland øvde i vår på å bruke et hemmelig våpen mot undersjøiske kabler, men operasjonen ved Svalbard ble avslørt og hindret av Norge og andre Nato-land, sier to vestlige tjenestemenn til Reuters.

Tjenestemennene sier russerne brukte dyptgående miniubåter for å simulere utplasseringen av avansert og ødeleggende teknologi. Den hemmelige øvelsen skal ha blitt gjennomført av Russlands direktorat for undersjøisk krigføring.

I en felles operasjon fulgte og konfronterte Nato-landene Norge, Storbritannia og USA russiske skip, sier de to tjenestemennene, som snakker med løfte om anonymitet. De russiske fartøyene ble forhindret fra å fullføre øvelsen og forlot deretter det aktuelle området.

I april avslørte Norge og Storbritannia at de hadde avdekket en hemmelig russisk operasjon i arktisk farvann. Oppdagelsen av det nye våpenet, stedet der operasjonen skjedde og USAs deltakelse har ikke vært omtalt tidligere.

articles.content:
Fem Høyre-ordførere fra Agder, samt fylkesordfører Arne Thomassen, er blant 37 Høyre-ordførere som krever samme erstatning for ofrene etter Alexander L. Kielland-ulykken som Nordsjødykkerne fikk.

Det ble flertall i Stortinget i fjor sommer for at ofrene skal få erstatning, men lite har skjedd. Flere overlevende og etterlatte har falt fra bare det siste året, og ordførerne advarer nå mot å skyve den 46 år gamle saken enda lenger ut i tid.

Alexander Kielland-ulykken

123 oljearbeidere mistte livet da oljeplattformen «Alexander Kielland» havarerte i Nordsjøen i 1980. Vraket av plattformen ble noen år etter senket på dypt vann. Flere overlevende og pårørende har bedt om ny granksning av ulykken.

articles.title: EXPLAINED: How to appeal an immigration rejection in Norway
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        The process of getting a residence permit or visa in Norway can be quite stressful at times. It can even end in your application being rejected. If that happens, here's what you can do.

It is not uncommon for the Norwegian immigration authorities to reject immigration requests. However, if that happens, know that you can appeal the decision.

If you decide to appeal, the embassy or the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) will reconsider your case – as long as you filed the appeal within the deadline specified in the UDI decision letter you received.

While relatively straightforward, the appeal process also has a rigid structure you must be aware of.

In this article, we will go through the steps and key information you need to know if you're appealing a UDI immigration decision in Norway.

Know that you can start an appeal case only if you're the actual applicant for immigration to Norway or if you have a power of attorney for the applicant in question.

This also applies to the applicant's family members and other close contacts in Norway – they will need a power of attorney to appeal on the applicant's behalf.

As of the time of writing, you need to appeal the UDI's decision within three weeks from the date when the decision has been received or when you should have become aware of the authorities' decision.

If you fail to gather all the documentation or information you want to include in your appeal within the deadline, you still need to submit the appeal within three weeks.

In such cases, explain that you will send over more information and documentation at a later date. The authorities will then give you two more weeks to gather and send over the said materials.

First off, you need to write a letter and explicitly explain which decision you are appealing and why you believe the authorities' decision is incorrect. You can write the letter in Norwegian or English.

You will need to sign the letter, scan or take a photograph of the signed letter, and upload it to the UDI's form for document submission (available here).

Make sure that you include any new information or documentation that might be relevant to your case.

After that, you'll be notified via email or SMS when the UDI receives your appeal.

Submitting an appeal is free of charge, and you can find more information on the waiting times on the UDI's website, here.

Note that if an embassy has made the decision in your immigration application, you will have to hand in your appeal to the said embassy. In such cases, you will need to consult the embassy's website for the waiting times that apply.

Important note: It's very important to provide new information or add documents that support your case. If you fail to provide such information or documentation, your appeal will likely fail.

After you've submitted your appeal, you need to wait for the UDI to reconsider your case.

There are two possible outcomes: either the UDI grants your appeal, or it forwards the case to the Immigration Appeals Board (UNE) - the appellate body for immigration and citizenship cases - for further consideration.

If the UDI forwards your case to UNE, you will be notified by email or SMS. The UNE will then consider your case again and either reject or grant your appeal.

If your UNE appeal is successful, then the UDI's rejection will no longer apply. However, if the UNE also rejects your appeal, you will have no other possibilities of appeal in Norway.

Note that the rules are a bit different if an embassy is reviewing your appeal – you can find out more details on the website of the embassy in question.

Can you reside in Norway while the appeal case is being processed?

If your immigration request (usually an application for a residence permit or visa) is rejected, you will normally be given a deadline for leaving the country.

Your official decision letter will state whether you have the right to stay in Norway during the review process and how long.

Generally, the deadline is three weeks. However, if you wish to stay in Norway while the immigration authorities review your appeal case, you can apply to remain in the country by invoking a deferred implementation of the decision.

If the authorities grant your request, you will be able to stay in Norway until the appeal has been processed. However, if they reject your request, you will have to leave the country within the specified deadline.

Know that there are special rules in place for people who have applied for a renewal or who have had their residence permit revoked. You can find more information about these rules here.

Also, in some cases, and only if certain conditions are met, you might have the right to have your legal or other necessary expenses related to the appeal process covered. The UDI has more information on the conditions that apply on its website.

Note that you can reapply one more time even if your immigration application was previously rejected – if you believe that you meet the requirements at a later time.

You can find more information on the re-application process on the UDI's website here.

articles.title: Why Trondheim is ranked the 6th happiest city in the world
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        The annual Happy City Index, put together by a global team of researchers has released its 2026 results. Trondheim secured 6th place globally and came out on top among Norwegian cities. What sets it apart?F

The sixth edition of the index, published by the Institute for Quality of Life, evaluated 251 cities using 64 indicators across six key areas: citizens, governance, environment, economy, health, and mobility.

The "Gold tier" distinction recognises the top 50 cities demonstrating high performance across all categories. As their website explains, these are urban areas that combine quality of life, sustainability, and long-term development strategies.

Nordic neighbours dominated the top of the global leaderboard once again, with Copenhagen taking 1st place and Helsinki in Finland securing 2nd.

Geneva in Switzerland placed 3rd, Sweden's Uppsala took 4th, and Tokyo came in 5th.

Trondheim was the top-ranked Norwegian city, taking 6th place.

Oslo, the capital, came in 14th place. Bergen and Stavanger also made the Gold tier, ranking 31st and 37th respectively.

Further down the ranking, outside the top 50, Drammen, a city close to the capital that has recently gained recognition for its ongoing investment and growth, landed in 65th place.

The city’s high placement is largely driven by its stable economy, affordable housing, good welfare support, and a great quality of life.

Trondheim’s GDP per capita is over £65,000 (around 815,000 kroner), which is almost twice the global average.

Figures show that living costs remain manageable. For example, the study reveals that residents spend an average of only 16 percent of their income on rent, compared with a global average of over 32 percent.

Along with a low unemployment rate of only 2.2 percent, this helps create a secure financial environment for both locals and internationals.

For international residents, Trondheim can be a particularly welcoming destination. As the data show, 90 percent of the population can communicate in a foreign language, compared with a global average of just 34 percent. This can make it easier for newcomers to settle in and to navigate the country when they arrive.

Safety remains one of Norway's proudest hallmarks, and Trondheim is a great example. The city has a very low crime rate, with zero intentional homicides per 100,000 residents, which is much lower than the global average.

Another key factor setting Trondheim apart from other cities around the world is its public health and social welfare system. People in Trondheim have a high life expectancy of 85.4 years and benefit from generous family policies, such as 59 weeks of paid parental leave (covering at least 50 percent of their salary).

The city is also a major hub for education and innovation, with a top-ranked university that offers tuition-free higher education.

Coupled with great air quality and a strong commitment to green mobility, all these factors make Trondheim a well-rounded and forward-thinking city.

What do you think of the ranking? Does Trondheim deserve its place among the world’s happiest cities?

articles.title: Norway repatriates 69 Russians from ship seized in Arctic
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Norwegian authorities said Tuesday they helped repatriate 69 Russians who got stranded in the Arctic after a Russian ship was seized at the demand of Ukrainian state energy group Naftogaz.

Norwegian authorities said Tuesday they helped repatriate 69 Russians who got stranded in the Arctic after a Russian ship was seized at the demand of Ukrainian state energy group Naftogaz.

Citing a Norwegian court order, the governor of Svalbard on September 2nd announced the seizure of the Professor Molchanov - a vessel used to shuttle people between Russia and Barentsburg, a Russian mining community in the Norwegian archipelago located 1,000 kilometres (621 miles) south of the North Pole.

"After good dialogue with the consul general of the Russian Federation in Barentsburg and representatives from (Russian state-owned coal mining company) Trust Arktikugol, the governor has today assisted 69 Russian citizens back to Russia," a statement from the governor's office said.

The Russian nationals returned via Kirkenes, a town in northern Norway near the Russian border, on Tuesday afternoon, it added.

The vessel was seized as Naftogaz sought $4.2 billion from Russia in compensation for the seizure of its assets following Moscow's 2014 annexation of Crimea.

In 2023, a Hague-based arbitration tribunal ruled in favour of the Ukrainian company, a ruling Norway recognises.

Naftogaz is seeking the sale of the vessel to cover part of its claim, but the Norwegian courts have postponed final decisions to give Russia the opportunity to challenge the seizure of the vessel.

The Russian embassy in Norway has already announced that it will appeal the decision handed down on August 31st by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court.

The financial dispute has also sparked diplomatic tensions.

Russia's embassy in Norway last week called for the vessels "immediate release", slamming the seizure as "a politically motivated violation of international law".

The Russian foreign ministry also summoned the Norwegian ambassador to Russia in Moscow.

Norwegian authorities meanwhile argue they are not "a party" in the case, and that Svalbard's governor is obliged to execute the court's order.

Svalbard is governed by a 1920 treaty, which while recognising Norwegian sovereignty also grants nationals of all the contracting parties the right to exploit natural resources there "on a footing of absolute equality".

Russia operates a coal mine in the village of Barentsburg, where around 350 Russian and Russian-speaking Ukrainians live, as well as another smaller settlement called Pyramiden.

articles.title: 'King Harald made immigrants welcome': How international residents view Norway’s royals
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        After King Harald V passed away, Norway has come together in national mourning. But what do the monarchy and this historic period of transition mean for the country’s international community? Readers shared their perspective in a survey conducted by The Local.

Every day, thousands of people have gathered at the Royal Palace in Oslo to leave flowers, cards, and tributes. Many have waited for hours to pay their last respects in the Royal Chapel, showing the nation’s deep love and affection for the late King Harald V.

Many people in the international community have also shared deep feelings of grief and sympathy for a monarch who, for some, came to define cultural unity and empathy in Norway.

To learn how foreign residents see the monarchy during this historic change, we asked our readers for their thoughts. Do they feel connected to the royal family? Do they follow royal news, value their traditional role, or feel indifferent or even opposed to the institution?

READ ALSO: Everything you need to know about King Harald V’s funeral in Oslo

Most international readers responded with deep respect and appreciation for the Norwegian Crown.​

For many international residents, Norway’s Royal Family plays an active role in their sense of belonging. Jane, 57, living in Bergen, called the monarchy "my hope," saying, "I hope that the people learn to embrace us foreigners as the monarchy seem to do."

​Sue shared a similar view. "King Harald made immigrants welcome but with sense. He informed everyone how the country is and what the country believes in," she said.

​For others, the royal family stands for national stability. Sven Huseby, 83, an Oslo resident who was born in Norway but lived much of his life abroad, said he has "tremendous respect for the royal family members who exercise their responsibilities as national uniters."

Carlos Yan, 72, living in Nøtterøy, put it simply: "I am Portuguese and totally support the Norwegian Royal family... Love them."

While many express strong respect, some feel distant or are troubled by recent royal controversies.

Aleksandar, 35, living in Oslo, explained that as a non-citizen, it is hard to relate to the institution. "I try to keep myself informed about all concerning aspects when it comes to the royal family, but as I am not a Norwegian citizen myself, I still cannot deeply relate."

He also criticized recent scandals that have put the royal family under public scrutiny. "I like the 'Alt for Norge' politics of the former and the future kings, but I was let down by Mette-Marit's connection to Jeffrey Epstein, the choice of partner of Märtha Louise, and the crimes committed by Marius Borg Høiby."

One anonymous respondent was even more critical: "If this is your first family that is an example to us all, I do not think I want to become Norwegian. I am disgusted by their behaviour and think Norway should become a republic!", though adding that "Haakon seems a good man."

Irena, 55, living in Oslo, maintained a more neutral position. "I have no feelings connecting the royal family and my national identity," she said.

When asked about specific royal events, many respondents pointed to May 17th (Constitution Day) as their main point of connection.

Aside from these annual celebrations, there weren't any other activities mentioned, which suggests that the royal family is most visible during big national holidays and less present in the daily lives of foreign residents.

What international residents expect from King Haakon VIII

As King Haakon VIII takes the throne, expectations are mixed but many are genuinely optimistic.

71-year-old Deborah, from Karmøy, said the new king "has big shoes to fill." Jane, 57, from Bergen, emphasized that "he will be a good leader as long as he stays with progressive leadership."

Aleksandar said he is confident about the new king and hopes he "will lead by example." Sue also mentioned that the new king and his wife will be good for the country.

Others, like Sam, 35, also living in the capital, said he is simply "optimistic of the new king's reign."

Overall, people describe King Haakon as a genuinely good man. "I hope he proves to be a worthy king," said one anonymous respondent.

Opari shared enthusiasm for the new reign: "I’m excited to see how it is to have King Haakon as our new king."

articles.content:

Ukraina

Ukraina er et land i Europa som grenser til Russland, Belarus, Polen, Moldova og Romania. Landet har nær 38 millioner innbyggere, ifølge data fra FN. I februar 2022 gikk Russland til fullskala invasjon – se emneknaggen «Krigen i Ukraina».

articles.title: Russia demands 'immediate release' of vessel seized by Norway
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Russia on Thursday demanded the "immediate release" of a Russian ship seized by Norway a day earlier in the Arctic at the demand of Ukrainian state energy group Naftogaz as compensation for asset seizures.

The governor of Svalbard, a Norwegian archipelago located 1,000 kilometres (621 miles) south of the North Pole, announced the seizure of the vessel, the Professor Molchanov, on Wednesday, September 2nd, citing an August 31st court order.

Naftogaz is seeking $4.2 billion from Russia as compensation for the seizure of its assets following Moscow's 2014 annexation of Crimea.

In 2023, a Hague-based arbitration tribunal ruled in favour of the Ukrainian company, a ruling Norway recognises.

The Professor Molchanov, a research vessel primarily used for expedition cruises, is currently stuck at the quay in Barentsburg, a mining settlement operated by Russia in Svalbard, pending a new decision by the governor or by the Norwegian courts, the governor's office said.

The Russian foreign ministry on Thursday said it had summoned the Norwegian ambassador to Russia, Heidi Olufsen, to lodge a "strong protest" over the seizure.

She was "informed that the Russian side categorically rejects not only the seizure of the Professor Molchanov but also the recent intensification of Norway's actions aimed at curtailing the legitimate Russian presence on the archipelago", the ministry said.

The Russian embassy in Norway condemned what it called "a politically motivated violation of international law" and announced it would lodge an appeal.

"We demand the immediate release of the vessel and that the safety of the passengers and crew be ensured," the embassy said in an email to AFP.

Norwegian authorities meanwhile said they are not "a party" in the case.

"As the authority responsible for enforcing court decisions, the governor of Svalbard is obliged to implement the court's ruling," Norwegian justice ministry spokesperson Frank Lynum told AFP.

"This applies to all cases of attachment and enforcement, regardless of the parties involved," he added, saying the issue was handled "in the ordinary way by the Norwegian courts".

Because of sanctions imposed by Norway after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the seized vessel is, according to the Russian embassy, the only supply channel for Russian settlements in Svalbard.

The Arctic archipelago is governed by a 1920 treaty.

While it recognises Norwegian sovereignty, the treaty also grants nationals of all the contracting parties the right to exploit natural resources there "on a footing of absolute equality".

Russia operates a coal mine in the village of Barentsburg, where around 350 Russian and Russian-speaking Ukrainian residents live, as well as another smaller settlement called Pyramiden.

Oslo stresses that the rights guaranteed by the treaty do not exempt other nationals or companies from complying with Norwegian laws and regulations.

articles.content:

Forsvaret skal bistå politiet i gjennomføringen av tiltakene, står det også.

Nærmere informasjon om hvilke områder som omfattes og hvilke tidsrom som gjelder, er publisert gjennom luftfartens ordinære informasjonskanaler.

articles.title: Norway's UDI immigration authority website hit by cyberattack
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        The website of the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) went offline on Friday, September 4th, after a cyberattack claimed by a pro-Russian hacker group.

The group, calling itself "Server Killers", claimed responsibility for the Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack, Norwegian media reported.

A DDoS attack occurs when multiple systems flood a target website with excessive traffic, causing the website to crash or become unavailable.

Earlier this week, the same group said it had carried out similar DDoS attacks on several Norwegian universities and colleges.

This incident comes at a time of growing concern about cybersecurity and threats aimed at public sector online services in recent weeks.

People attempting to access the official portal are met with error messages.

This means that anyone looking to obtain information on Norwegian immigration or submit paperwork will be unable to do so until the authorities resolve the issue.

UDI has not yet said when the website will return to normal and services will be restored.

articles.title: Grindr inngår gigantforlik etter hiv-søksmål
articles.content:
Datingappen Grindr har gått med på å betale 26 millioner pund til brukere som saksøkte appen for deling av ekstremt sensitiv persondata, deriblant hiv-status, med reklameselskaper.

Søksmålet ble tatt ut av advokatfirmaet Austen Hays i april 2024 på vegne av 12.000 personer, skriver The Guardian.

Om de 26 millioner pundene (327 millioner kroner) blir fordelt likt på alle de 12.000, mottar hver person 2167 pund (cirka 27.245 kroner).

Grindr er en datingapp for skeive og hevder å ha opptil 15 millioner brukere verden over.

Ifølge søksmålet foregikk delingen av brukernes hiv-status og andre sensitive detaljer fram til 2020, mens selskapet var eid av et kinesisk selskap.

Selskapet har fått flere store bøter i Norge for lignende personvernsbrudd.

Forbrukerrettigheter

EU har vedtatt nye rettigheter for forbrukere som kjøper digitale tjenester og innhold. De vil også gjelde i Norge, opplyser Forbrukertilsynet. Ifølge de nye reglene skal garantier gjelde så lenge man er abonnent og kan ikke vare kortere enn to år.

articles.title: AfD: – Et drømmeresultat
articles.content:
Alice Weidel, en av lederne i ytre høyre-partiet Alternativ for Tyskland (AfD) beskriver nattens valgseier i delstaten Sachsen-Anhalt som et drømmeresultat.

Partiet ser ut til ende med rundt 44 prosent av stemmene i den tidligere østtyske delstaten, og Weidel hevder resultatet viser at folk vil ha endring i den politiske kursen for landet.

Weidel sier partiets neste mål er å nå 40 prosent i det neste valget på nasjonalt nivå.

Selv om AfD fikk suverent flest stemmer i delstaten, som har vel to millioner innbyggere, klarer de ikke få flertall alene i delstatsforsamlingen. Dermed er det ikke gitt at de vil overta styringen fordi andre partier nekter å samarbeide med dem på grunn av svært kontroversielle synspunkter.

En brakseier i tysk delstatsvalg sender sjokkbølger gjennom Europa. Dette er landets første ytre høyre-seier siden 2. verdenskrig.
